You can rage, uninstall, swear you’re never playing again… then 10 minutes later, “Find Match.” 😂

Dota 2 may test your patience, but that’s also what makes every victory feel so satisfying.

10/10. Would rage again. 🎮🔥

The game is good and even legendary per se. But there are crucial aspects that would make me never come back to this game. 
One of them is the non-healthy community that doesn`t bring you anything but additional distress and unwillingness to contact with other players what is extremely crucial in a game that is considered to be a team-orientiered. Instead of useful communication that leads you and your team towards victory you will gain (almost always) lectures how you should play and how your skill (therefore your life too) is miserable etc. And it`s still on 12 000 behavior and communication score.
The second reason is enldess updates and changes for just changes. I have a strong feeling that developers don`t update the game and change mechanics/heroes/items/map etc. countless amount of times for making the game better. No, they do it just for the fact of changing itself. It`s difficult to explain the point (since I don`t mind that the game becomes better for players)
The third reason - it`s a learning curve. I hit almost 5000 MMR in 3000 hours (and I have never had a goal to grind MMR, I just play for the proccess itself) and at this rating I feel already uncomfortable. The higher rating I get the more unwillingness to play I have because the game is turning into dirty pit where the goal is not getting enjoyment from the game but compete and always forcing to prove your skill. It`s not the problem of the game itself (as I mentioned before I consider DOTA2 a legendary) but this pushes me away from getting back to it

testCases.rawText:
Dota 2 is not just a game—it’s a full-time job where nobody pays you, your coworkers blame you for everything, and your boss is a Russian guy playing Techies with a broken microphone.

The gameplay is simple: choose a hero, buy some items, destroy towers, and slowly lose your mental health. Every match starts with “good luck, have fun” and ends with four people arguing about who fed first.

The community is incredibly friendly. They will teach you new words in several languages, remind you that your parents are disappointed, and offer strategic advice such as:

“Delete the game.”
“Uninstall life.”
“Report mid.”
“Why no gank?”
The matchmaking system is also amazing. You can be a peaceful support player, minding your own business, and somehow get matched with a carry who has played 7,000 hours but still doesn’t know what a ward is.

Every game is an emotional journey. You experience hope, confidence, confusion, rage, acceptance, and finally queue again because surely the next match will be different.

It won’t.

Dota 2 has beautiful graphics, incredible strategy, hundreds of unique heroes, and the ability to turn your closest friends into sworn enemies within 30 seconds.

Would recommend to anyone who enjoys strategy games, psychological warfare, and suffering. Easiest 10/10 of my life.

testCases.rawText:
I’ve been playing Dota 2 since 2013.

No other game is as fun as Dota 2, but the inverse is also true: no other game has given me this much frustration and grief. I have invested many hours of my life into this game, and I do not regret it.

I've made genuine connections through this game that turned into real-life friendships. Ultimately, this game is best played with friends. In its current state, Dota 2 needs to be friendlier to new players. I can enjoy the game given I have 6,000+ hours across various accounts, but the steep initial investment pushes people away from wanting to learn.

Dota 2 is a fantastic game, and I highly recommend it. Just know that if you want to play, it requires a huge time investment—one that is made much easier when you play with a friend. Once that learning curve is over, you'll start seeing yourself improve and get a satisfaction that few other games can match.

testCases.rawText:
Dota 2 is a free to play MOBA that originally started it's life as a mod in Warcraft 3. I want to start off this review by saying that this game is very complex, while you can learn the basics of the game in a few matches the underlying mechanics will take you many hundred to understand. If your looking for something to pick up and play this probably isn't it unless your willing to learn over a hundred hours or more. The game is free to play but unlike other free to play games all purchases in Dota are purely cosmetic and add no advantage or pay to win mechanics, as more games should be.

For those unfamiliar a MOBA consists a 5v5 game on a 3 lane map. 2 heroes go top and bottom and 1 usually will go middle. There a certain heroes who excel in certain roles that you will eventually learn over time. In recent years Dota has added a new player learning section which is great for people new to MOBAs or Dota in general. It covers not just a MOBA but also mechanics specific to Dota I will take about later. A typical match in Dota will last between 30 and 75 minutes but have lasted all the way up to close to over 3 hours in a pro level match before. There are so many different mechanics that have an impact on a match that no 2 matches will ever feel the same.

For the majority of my review I will be comparing Dota 2 to it's main competitor League of Legends and then I will get into other details on Dota after. For starters Dota 2  has far less heroes than League of Legends at 127 currently compared to 171 in League of Legends. Despite needing to learn more heroes League of Legends is actually an easier MOBA to play, however because of that fact it's also boring and games are pretty predictable. If you lose the laning phase it's very hard to come back in League of Legends because there are no game changing items you can buy. In Dota 2 there are items such as Black King Bar (BKB) which makes you 100% immune to magic damage, which is 1 of the 3 types of damage from hero abilities in Dota. There are other items to like the blink dagger which allows you to teleport a certain distance around you to gank enemies. There are many different items in Dota that can allow you to come back from a few deaths at the start of the game. You also don't lose gold when you die in league making getting items a little easier where as in Dota you lose a % of gold and the other team gets gold each kill.

In League of Legends the laning phase also changes to 2 bottom 1 top 1 mid and 1 jungle right away which is roaming the map and killing the mobs for gold and xp. In Dota even the high damage carry heroes need a few levels before being able to farm the jungle. In League of Legends you also don't have camp stacking. In Dota when farming jungle or in the early game the support heroes and sometimes mid will go around and pull jungle mobs from there spawn. If they are out of the spawn box at the start of each new minute a new stack will spawn and if you run away from the pulled mobs they will return effectively leaving 2 groups on the jungle camp. The person who makes the stacked camp gets XP and Gold once those are killed even if not by themselves. This is just another big mechanic in Dota that allows you to come back or get ahead of the other team.

Dota has much more mechanics to watch for in the laning phase as well such as "Denying" or killing your own creeps before the other team does. This will give the other team half the XP they normally would and denies them getting gold from the last hit. Both games feature the same last hit mechanics requiring you to be the final person to hit a creep to their death to get any gold. However in league there is no turn rate so u don't need to face the creep to hit it where as in Dota each hero has its own timing to turn and face the creep and it's own timing to hit the creep you will need to account for. Again this is just another way to get an advantage back to your team if you die in the laning phase, just getting more last hits and denying the other teams gold and XP will help.

Lastly Dota 2 is harder because you can't see over stairs. The game uses a 3D model where league you can basically see anywhere expect hiding in a bush or something. Enemies can be waiting at the top of the stairs and you wouldn't know without climbing up or placing wards to see. This makes movement very different in Dota and can lead to some bad deaths and emphasizes the importance of placing wards for vision. Dota also applies a 25% chance to miss your target such as a creep if they are above you, this is most common for the midlaner who fights between 2 stairs.

While these mechanics make the game far more challenging to play and learn, they do create many options for a game to turn out and for that I rate it a 10/10 for game mechanics. The game gets a new update about once a month constantly balancing heroes and changing the content and mechanics in the game. This is frustrating to learn all the time but also keeps the game ever changing and well balanced as it's hard to make 127 heroes feel perfectly balanced. It also shows the devs care a lot about the game.

Dota 2 has had a huge esports scene in the past but for some reason they decided to make a couple large tournaments throughout the year rather than host The International (TI) as a big event. Personally I think this is a 1/10. As someone who didn't play much Dota in the past the big TI prize pools caught my eye and brought in new players like myself to see what this game is all about. I think if Valve wants to make different tournaments have decent prize pools go back to the old model of community funded battle passes and cosmetics to go back to the prize pool and just host multiple passes throughout the year for different tournaments. The tournaments are still large but it does attract media away from Dota and towards other titles with higher payouts as well as gamers and teams trying to make a profitable living. Look how many people were playing Fortnite and head of the game over their 100M dollar tournament years ago. Steam should be advertising the tournament on their store page when it was 20-40M for the TI. It's a big deal and the qualifier rounds and main tournament coverage should be posted to attract new viewers and players.

Overall Dota is a great game, it falls in line with Valves other games like Counter Strike in the fact that it is easy to run. Valve also has 2 giants in the market making them a ton of revenue on top of steam sales commissions that this game isn't going anywhere anytime soon. I would recommend playing this game and trying to learn it for 100 hours which will allow you to finally play the ranked mode and get matched with people around the same skill as you. Don't worry about people getting mad with you while you learn, and maybe try a couple bot games first before unranked. This game is challenging but is super fun.

I've played DotA since over 20 years ago.  This iteration has smooth graphics and everything and the game is great...  that's not the problem.

How is there not a surrender option in this game?  For a game that by definition takes a LONG time to play a match, it's a little obnoxious to have to play a clearly losing game for 30-60 minutes just not to get punished.  I am adult with things to do, I am not investing my time in sitting around and pretending to play just to placate your crappy system.  And when you do get punished?  You have to win two single draft games to get out of time-out.  The problem is that no one is playing that you sit in matchmaking for 10 minutes before giving up and realizing this game has a SERIOUS systemic blind spot. 

I'd argue it was better when people just left and that was that - the remaining players scaled quicker as a result and created a different strategic situation when that happened.  I get serious punishments for ranked play, but for casual unranked?  Be real.  This is a game, not my job.

Way to ruin a classic.

testCases.rawText:
[h2]The Undisputed King of Competitive Gaming[/h2]
Having walked the long road from the original WC3 DotA, through the early days of Dota 2 and the Reborn update, right up to the current patch, I can state this with absolute certainty: Dota 2 was, is, and likely always will be one of the most intense and deeply rewarding competitive games ever created.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3763540634
[h2]The Duality of the Community[/h2]
There is almost [b]no in-between.[/b]

The matchmaking experience here is a perfect, [b]chaotic 50/50 split.[/b] Every match is a literal coin toss. You will either get a whiny man-child who didn't get his mid lane, instantly destroys his items at minute zero, and marches down the lane to feed — or you will be blessed with an incredibly competent, understanding team that knows exactly how to play the game (ideally, in absolute, telepathic silence).

[h2]True Free-to-Play[/h2]
Unlike many modern titles, the monetization here is genuinely optional. The game constantly showers you with bonuses and drops. You can play completely free of charge without spending a single dime, and you will still watch your inventory naturally fill up with sweet cosmetic sets and skins.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3764613733
[h2]The Arcade Universe[/h2]
It's literally a whole [b]different game within a game.[/b]

The Arcade section isn't just a feature; it's a thriving multiverse of its own. This is the legendary breeding ground for massive hits like Auto Chess and Custom Hero Clash, drawing [b]tens of thousands of concurrent players[/b] just to have fun.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3764780833
[h2]Justice Finally Served[/h2]
And the absolute [b]cherry on top?[/b] Surprisingly, the report system actually works now. Toxic behavior genuinely gets punished, making the MMR grind far more bearable.

testCases.rawText:
## How to fix Dota 2

* Remove half the jungle camps
* Bring back Unique Attack Modifiers so carries have to choose
* Give more spell-based counterplay while also increasing cooldowns
* Make mana pools something you have to carefully manage again.
* Go back to 6 slots total. No backpack, no scroll slot.
* Rollback the last 8 years of absurd power creep. Only idiots want every patch to be nothing but buffs.
* Remove healing lotuses and wisdom shrines.
* Rework tormentor. If you want it to be a true goal that dictates a team's movements, it should give something more significant than an aghs shard to a random teammate. Give a team a tower they can choose to deploy where one of theirs has died. Make it so the same tower cannot be resurrected more than once.
* Allow players (whose heroes are still alive) to aim tower aggro at enemy heroes, as it is much too easy for experienced players to manipulate tower aggro, while inexperienced players aren't going to have any notion of it. So give the inexperienced players some counterplay.
* Bounty runes are not a bad idea, but they're largely an afterthought. Return them back into the cycle at the main two rune spawn points. There shouldn't be a guarantee of getting a potent combat-oriented rune every time. Make it mean more when someone gets a double damage.
* While we're on the subject, return it to being double damage, and make that double damage extend to spell damage. If PA can get to a point of cleaving a whole team for 4000 damage with a crit without a rune, then high damage ults on heroes like Zeus or Lion should also have the opportunity to put out damage like that if they end up being lucky enough to net the rune that will allow that. It won't break the game, and certainly no more than the currently broken and uninteresting state the game is currently in.
* Add many more trees and make them stay dead longer after a certain point. Leave the tree respawn rate alone during the first 10 minutes, and then make it longer after that. The reason is simple - players should have meaningful counterplay against heroes with a need/usage of trees, but it should be carefully measured so those heroes aren't dumpstered in the laning phase because of this.
* And finally, to add to the tree changes, make more items able to destroy larger amounts of trees. Destructible environments with meaning and purpose to strategic destruction where it matters is more interesting than the tertiary purpose of trees now as mere hindrances for line of sight that have been significantly reduced. Some of the coolest plays in dota are jukes where people used trees and branches to their advantage.

The theme is, of course, COUNTERPLAY. Bludgeoning real counterplay out of the game through arbitrary changes over many years that have caused absurd power creep to just get more and more silly is why the game fails to hold the interest of players for much longer than the time it takes for the new from the last major patch to wear off. Make it mean more to really learn the game again.

Thanks for coming to my TED talk.

The learning curve is ridiculously steep, and the game does very little to make new players feel welcome. In a normal match or Turbo, you can get flamed for practically anything placing a ward in the wrong spot, missing a creep, buying the wrong item, picking the “wrong” hero, making a bad play, or simply not knowing something that a veteran player considers obvious. And, of course, there is always the possibility of running into a smurf who will completely destroy you and then proceed to mock you for the entire game.If you are genuinely interested in learning Dota 2, I would actually recommend spending your first 50 hours simply getting familiar with as many heroes as possible. You obviously won't master every hero, item, macro decision, and micro mechanic within 100 hours that would be completely unrealistic. Even after hundreds of hours, there will still be plenty you don't understand.At the end of the day, though, Dota 2 is a game, so don't forget to have fun.Although, realistically, the only person having fun might be the smurf on the enemy team. testCases.rawText:
Dota 2 Review — 4,000 hours — Recommended (I guess)

4,000 hours. Let me repeat that. FOUR THOUSAND HOURS. That's 166 days of my life. I could have learned the violin, built a house, or watched my hair grow. Instead, I pulled it out.

I used to be competitive. Very competitive. I screamed at my teammates so much my neighbors thought I was being robbed every night at 11 PM. I lost faith in humanity around hour 800. By hour 2,000, I was convinced my teammates were losing on purpose ,a secret organization of psychos assigned specifically to MY team, every game, just to make me mad. Valve knows what I'm talking about. The matchmaking algorithm has a folder with my name on it.

i m 50 years old now
But here's the thing: I changed. I found peace. I don't scream anymore. I don't play carry anymore. I play support now, and I have discovered the true meaning of Dota:

I feed the enemy carry all game long.

And you know what? He's having a GREAT time. Best game of his life. Rampage at minute 20. Somewhere out there, a 14-year-old is smiling because of me.

After 4,000 hours, I finally learned the most important lesson this game can teach: you can't make your team happy. But you CAN make someone happy.

10/10. Would lose faith in humanity again.

testCases.rawText:
Dota 2 is one of the best games ever made — and also one of the hardest to recommend without a warning label. It has a massive, thriving player base with millions of concurrent users, a thriving esports scene, and a level of depth that few games can match. But it is also brutally complex, unforgiving to newcomers, and demanding in a way that can feel overwhelming.

The Good: A Game That Rewards Dedication

The core of Dota 2 is sublime. Every match is a chess game played at real-time speed, where decisions matter, teamwork is essential, and the skill ceiling is essentially infinite. The game is free-to-play with no pay-to-win mechanics, which is remarkable given its scale. The hero pool is enormous — over 100 characters, each with unique abilities, roles, and playstyles — and the item system, map dynamics, and meta shifts keep the game fresh even after thousands of hours. When everything clicks, Dota 2 delivers a sense of satisfaction that few other games can match. The million-plus online count is proof that this formula works.

The Bad: A Mountain of Complexity

Here is the catch: Dota 2 is incredibly hard to learn. The mechanics are deep and layered — last-hitting, denying, creep aggro, stacking, pulling, ward placement, timings, power spikes, and dozens of other systems that are never explained properly in-game. Then there is the hero problem: with 100+ characters, each having multiple abilities, remembering what every single one does is a massive undertaking. You need to know not just your own hero, but every enemy hero's abilities, cooldowns, and counters. That knowledge gap is brutal for new players.

The learning curve is less a curve and more a cliff. The game does have a tutorial, but it barely scratches the surface. Most players learn through trial, error, and a lot of frustration — often while being flamed by teammates. It is not a game you can casually pick up and enjoy immediately. It demands time, patience, and a willingness to lose repeatedly while you figure things out.

Verdict!

Dota 2 is a masterpiece of game design, but it is not for everyone. If you are willing to invest the time to learn its complex mechanics and memorize the abilities of over 100 heroes, you will find one of the deepest and most rewarding competitive games in existence. If you want something you can learn in a weekend, look elsewhere. It is brilliant, it is massive, and it is merciless — and that is exactly why its community loves it!

testCases.rawText:
Dota is the purest love-hate relationship I've ever had with a game. Every match somehow leaves you frustrated, exhausted, and still wanting to queue again. One game you get the best teammates ever and everything just works, then the next game you get the kind of team that makes you hate the match, hate the game, and for a few minutes, hate everyone in it.

Losing can feel miserable, winning can feel euphoric, and both still make you want to play one more.

With friends though, this game can be absolutely amazing and some of the best fun you'll have. So for newcomers, expect psychological torture, countless hours of your life gone, an unhealthy attachment to a game you'll swear you hate, while still being one of the best competitive experiences you'll ever have.

And at the time of writing this, The International 2026 begins tomorrow. All my wishes to Falcons to lift the Aegis!

Dota 2 — A Masterpiece That Can Drive You Insane

Dota 2 is one of the deepest and most rewarding competitive games ever made. After spending a significant amount of time playing it, you start to realize that this is not just a MOBA about destroying the enemy Ancient. It is a game of strategy, psychology, teamwork, mechanics, and decision-making, where even the smallest mistake can cost you the entire match.

✅ What Makes Dota 2 Great

Insane strategic depth. The combination of hero drafts, item builds, counters, map control, vision, rotations, and team fights makes every match unique. There is always something new to learn, regardless of your experience.

Incredible hero diversity. The roster offers an enormous variety of playstyles. Every hero has its own strengths, weaknesses, and potential, and the right combination of abilities can completely change the outcome of a game.

High skill ceiling. Dota 2 rewards game knowledge, mechanical skill, positioning, timing, and smart decision-making. Winning through experience and understanding the game feels genuinely satisfying.

Unforgettable comebacks. Few things compare to turning around a seemingly impossible game with one perfectly executed team fight or by punishing a critical enemy mistake.

Regular updates and evolving strategies. Balance patches and gameplay changes keep the experience fresh and force players to adapt instead of relying on the same strategies forever.

Free-to-play done right. All heroes are available without grinding to unlock them or purchasing them individually. The competitive gameplay remains accessible to everyone.

❌ The Problems

Toxicity. Flaming, blaming, griefing, and teammates giving up prematurely can ruin even the best matches. Sometimes the hardest part of Dota 2 is not defeating the enemy team but maintaining your composure.

Inconsistent matchmaking. Some games feel balanced and competitive, while others seem decided by the difference in team coordination long before the final fight.

A brutal learning curve. New players face an overwhelming amount of information, from hundreds of abilities and item interactions to advanced macro decisions. Dota 2 demands patience and dedication.

Frustrating team dependency. Individual skill matters, but this is still a team game. You can make the right decisions and play your role well without being able to compensate for every mistake made by four other players.

Long matches and mental fatigue. A single game can demand a serious investment of time and concentration. Losing after a long, hard-fought match can be exhausting, especially in ranked.

Balance and meta issues. Some patches make certain heroes or strategies feel disproportionately strong. Adapting is part of the experience, but not every meta is equally enjoyable.

⚡Final Thoughts

Dota 2 is a game that can be incredibly frustrating and unbelievably satisfying, sometimes within the same match. It tests your patience, punishes your mistakes, rewards your knowledge, and constantly reminds you that there is always room for improvement.

Despite its flaws, the depth of its gameplay is exceptional. The satisfaction of mastering a difficult hero, outsmarting your opponents, coordinating a perfect team fight, or winning a match that seemed completely lost is what keeps the game compelling in the long run.

It is definitely not a game for everyone. If you want something casual, relaxing, and consistently fair, Dota 2 might test your patience. But if you enjoy competitive challenges, strategic freedom, and a game with an incredibly high skill ceiling, there is hardly anything quite like it.

Dota 2 is not perfect, and sometimes it makes you question your sanity. But when everything clicks, it reminds you why you keep coming back.

Final rating: 9/10.

A legendary competitive game with unmatched strategic depth, endless replayability, and a community that can be both its greatest strength and its biggest weakness.

GG WP. See you on the battlefield.

Unfair Punishment System Is Ruining Dota 2

I have spent a significant amount of time and money on Dota 2, but I am extremely disappointed with the current punishment system.

The game repeatedly gives me Low Priority penalties, ranked matchmaking restrictions, and reduces my Behavior Score and Communication Score, even when the situation involves temporary technical issues rather than intentional misconduct.

Sometimes my internet connection drops or my computer freezes. I always try to reconnect within a few minutes, but the system still treats me as if I deliberately abandoned the game.

In one of my recent matches, I was simply taking my time to choose a hero. I was still connected to the game, yet I received another penalty.

My Behavior Score and Communication Score have now dropped to critically low levels, making the overall matchmaking experience increasingly frustrating.

The worst part is that the system creates a vicious cycle: once your scores drop, recovering them becomes extremely difficult.

I regularly purchase in-game items and have financially supported this game because I genuinely enjoy Dota 2. However, spending money on a game that repeatedly punishes you without properly considering the circumstances feels incredibly disappointing.

Valve needs to seriously reconsider how its automated punishment system works. There should be a clear distinction between intentional griefing, abandoning games on purpose, and temporary technical difficulties.

Players deserve transparency, fairness, and the opportunity to appeal questionable penalties.

I cannot recommend Dota 2 in its current state.

Until Valve improves its punishment system and starts taking legitimate player complaints seriously, my review will remain negative.

testCases.rawText:
I installed Dota 2 expecting a competitive multiplayer game.

What I received was an unpaid apprenticeship in human suffering.

There are games where you learn mechanics, improve your reflexes, develop strategies, and eventually become better than you were before. Dota takes a more ambitious approach. It attempts to reconstruct your entire personality from the ground up.

You begin with confidence.

You select a hero. You buy your starting items. You walk towards the lane with the quiet optimism of someone who has absolutely no idea what is about to happen.

Ten minutes later, your Russian teammate is furiously typing because you didn't rotate.

You don't know what he is saying, but you understand the emotional meaning.

Apparently you have committed an international crime.

This is one of Dota's greatest features: the extraordinary diversity of human personalities you encounter. There is always one player who has been waiting their entire life for this particular match and will personally investigate every mistake you have made since the moment you installed Steam.

Miss one last hit?

Reported.

Die to a gank?

Reported.

Buy the wrong item?

Reported.

Exist in the same geographical region as Russia?

Probably reported.

And yet, somehow, the same people who are threatening to uninstall the game, abandon the match, and report the entire team will still be playing another game approximately fourteen seconds after the Ancient explodes.

Then there are the specialists.

The carry who has spent 38 minutes farming and suddenly announces that the team needs to "play around me."

The support who has purchased approximately 14 wards but has placed all of them in locations where absolutely nothing has ever happened.

The mid player who dies twice and immediately begins constructing a legal case against the position 4.

The offlaner who has been missing since minute six.

And the mysterious player who says "trust me" immediately before doing something that results in four deaths.

Somehow, despite all of this, you continue playing.

Because every once in a while, Dota produces a moment so perfectly coordinated that you briefly understand why millions of people willingly subject themselves to this game.

A smoke.

A perfect initiation.

Five enemy heroes caught.

Spells flying everywhere.

Your entire team screaming in celebration.

The enemy Ancient falls.

For a brief and beautiful moment, everyone loves each other.

Then you queue again.

And this is where Dota becomes truly impressive.

It doesn't matter how many times you swear that this is your last game. Dota has perfected the psychological art of making you believe that the next match will be different.

It won't.

The next match will contain another Russian who is somehow both your teammate and your sworn enemy.

Another person will type "gg" at minute eight.

Someone will disconnect.

Someone will buy an item that makes no sense.

Someone will blame you for something that happened on the opposite side of the map.

And you will sit there at 2:17 in the morning thinking:

"Surely we can win the next one."

Dota 2 is not a game you finish.

It is a cycle you enter.

You lose.

You blame your team.

Your team blames you.

You promise never to play again.

You queue again.

You win.

You experience an indescribable feeling of superiority.

You queue again.

You lose.

And somewhere in the distance, a Russian player is typing something in all chat that is probably not appropriate for this review.

10/10.

testCases.rawText:
Too Many Heroes, Too Much to Learn 😂

I wanted to like Dota 2, but the learning curve completely destroyed my patience.

There are so many heroes, abilities, items and strategies that getting started can feel less like playing a game and more like studying for an exam.

I also noticed that newer players often seem to pick the simpler heroes, which honestly makes sense. When you're still trying to understand what's happening, playing a hero with a complicated kit probably isn't helping. 💀

The good thing is that all heroes are free, so the problem isn't unlocking them — it's actually learning what all of them do.

The game clearly has an enormous amount of depth, and I can understand why people spend thousands of hours playing it.

But I didn't have the patience to learn enough of the game to comfortably play against more experienced players.

Dota 2 isn't a bad game — it's just a game that asks for more patience than I have. 😂

If you love competitive games with tons of strategy and don't mind a huge learning curve, you'll probably have a great time.

For me?

Not Recommended.

testCases.rawText:
An absolute masterpiece of competitive strategy that offers thousands of hours of unmatched depth—if your sanity can survive it.

Valve’s flagship MOBA stands as the absolute pinnacle of competitive gaming depth. With over 120 unique heroes, hundreds of items, and complex mechanics like creep denying, high-ground vision, buybacks, and dynamic map objectives, no two matches ever play out the same way. The sheer high-dopamine rush of pulling off a game-winning 5-man Black Hole, executing a clutch Aegis steal, or turning around a 60-minute mega-creep comeback provides a high that virtually no other multiplayer title can replicate. It is a game of pure, unadulterated skill where tactical macro-play, item customization, and split-second reaction times matter vastly more than raw mechanical reflexes.

However, that exact depth creates an absurdly intimidating brick wall for newcomers and casuals. The learning curve is not just steep; it is a vertical cliff that takes hundreds of hours of trial and error just to understand basic positioning and lane matchups. To make matters worse, the ranked matchmaking ecosystem can be notoriously toxic, where a single bad play or missed ability can trigger a wave of angry pinging and mic-screaming teammates. Compounding the learning curve is Valve's habit of constantly shifting the goalposts—massive gameplay overhauls routinely rework hero innate abilities, map layouts, and fundamental mechanics, forcing long-time players to constantly relearn the game from scratch.

Yet, despite the rage-inducing losses and complex updates, Dota 2 remains one of the most generous free-to-play packages on Steam. Unlike competing titles in the genre, every single hero is unlocked completely free from the moment you install the game—no grinding or paywalls required. Monolithic lore events, battle passes, and custom arcade maps keep the meta feeling fresh year after year. It is a volatile, high-stakes digital drug that will make you swear off playing forever, only to have you queueing up for "one last match" twenty minutes later.

9/10 — I spent 2,000 hours learning how to properly stack neutral creeps, got flamed in three different languages during a 70-minute loss, and immediately hit 'Find Match' again. The greatest competitive abusive relationship in gaming history.

testCases.rawText:
[h3]This genuinely has become one of the worst games I've ever played.[/h3]

[b]Valve no longer respects your time or patience.[/b]

[hr]

[h2]Dota 2[/h2]

Dota’s biggest problem for me is the [b]behavior and communication system.[/b]

The idea behind punishing genuinely toxic players is completely reasonable. The problem is that the system often feels incapable of distinguishing between someone who is actually abusive and someone who simply had a bad game.

You can underperform, have a terrible match, make repeated mistakes, or simply become the target of frustrated teammates, and suddenly you can be [b]mass-reported.[/b] The consequences can include losing access to communication features, even though [b]poor performance and toxic behavior are two completely different things.[/b]

That is incredibly frustrating in a game such as Dota that relies so heavily on team-play. People are going to have bad games. People are going to make mistakes. Sometimes you’re going to get completely [i]shit on[/i] and outplayed.

[b]None of those things should automatically make someone a candidate for losing their ability to communicate.[/b]

What makes the system worse is the lack of transparency.

You literally [b]cannot get help from Steam or Dota support.[/b] They will not help you. I have tried multiple times to find out why my score has fallen so much, only to get the most generic copy-and-paste replies.

So good luck fixing the issue.

Good luck finding out what you actually did wrong.

Good luck figuring out what you can actually do to resolve the situation.

When the obviously automated system gets something wrong — [b]which it can and does[/b] — there is absolutely no way for the player to challenge that decision, or even find out why the decision was made in the first place.

[hr]

Dota is already an extremely demanding game.

You have to learn hundreds of interactions, understand constantly changing strategies, coordinate with four other players, and deal with the enormous amount of information being thrown at you every match.

The last thing the game needs is a behavior system that makes players afraid that one bad stretch of games could affect their ability to communicate or even just play in general.

And that's before getting into:

[list]
[*]Griefing
[*]Smurfing
[*]Matchmaking frustrations
[*]And the fact that these problems have existed for far too long
[/list]

I don't expect Valve to eliminate every toxic player from Dota.

[b]That's impossible.[/b]

I expect the systems designed to deal with those players to be [b]accurate, transparent, and fair.[/b]

[hr]

[h2]Counter-Strike 2[/h2]

I know this is a review for Dota 2, but I have just had it [b]up to here[/b] with every aspect of Valve.

So let's just get into it.

Counter-Strike has a completely different set of problems, but the underlying issue is similar:

[b]Players have increasingly little confidence in the systems that are supposed to protect the competitive experience.[/b]

[h3]Cheating[/h3]

Cheating is obviously the biggest example.

For a competitive shooter where the entire experience depends on players believing that the people they're playing against are legitimate, confidence in anti-cheat is absolutely fundamental.

When players repeatedly encounter suspicious players and don't feel confident that those players will actually be caught, it damages the entire competitive environment — and leads to even more hackers.

If a completely innocent and legitimate player queues up for 50 matches, and out of those 50, even 10 of them had someone hacking, this leaves a small wedge in some players' minds that the only way to combat them is to [b]hack themselves.[/b]

Now what do we have?

[h3]A hacker producer.[/h3]

Every 100 new players that attempt to get into CS2 will either give up after 10 games, or succumb to hacking just to keep up.

[b]That is how you destroy the integrity of a competitive game.[/b]

[hr]

Then there are smurfs, griefers, matchmaking frustrations, and the overall inconsistency of the competitive experience.

Counter-Strike doesn't need to be perfect.

No anti-cheat system will ever catch every cheater immediately, and no matchmaking system will create perfectly balanced games every time.

But players need to believe that Valve is [b]aggressively fighting these problems.[/b]

When it becomes blatantly obvious that the developers behind the scenes do not care, why should the players?

Every suspicious death becomes another reason to become part of the problem, or to wonder whether the match was legitimate in the first place.

[b]That's incredibly damaging to a competitive game.[/b]

And once again, Valve has the resources to do better.

They have the resources to do [b]so, so much better.[/b]

Counter-Strike is one of the biggest competitive shooters in the world.

This isn't some obscure game with a tiny development team trying to survive.

Valve has an enormous amount of money, infrastructure, data, and experience behind it.

[hr]

[h2]The Bigger Problem With Valve[/h2]

This is what bothers me most about both games.

The problems aren't necessarily identical, but the pattern feels identical:

[h3][b]Valve seems increasingly comfortable letting fundamental problems exist as long as the games remain profitable.[/b][/h3]

And why wouldn't they be?

People continue spending hundreds or even thousands of dollars on cosmetics.

Steam continues generating enormous amounts of revenue.

Dota and Counter-Strike continue attracting massive player bases.

[b]There is very little financial incentive to completely overhaul systems that players constantly complain about when those same players continue spending money anyway.[/b]

I want Valve to invest in the foundations of these games.

I want Dota's behavior systems to be more transparent and better at distinguishing toxicity from simply playing badly.

I want Counter-Strike's competitive integrity systems to inspire confidence rather than suspicion.

I want matchmaking, reporting, anti-cheat, communication systems, and moderation to feel like they were designed around [b]protecting the player experience[/b] rather than simply automating problems away.

[hr]

Valve built its reputation by making games that felt years ahead of everyone else.

That's why it's so disappointing to see two of its most important games reach a point where so many players feel ignored.

[h2]The golden age of Valve is long past.[/h2]

But maybe it doesn't have to stay that way.

[b]But as long as players continue handing Valve money regardless of how these games are maintained, I don't see much reason for the company to change.[/b]

[h3]GG, Valve. gg.[/h3]

10/10 would recommend, 10/10 would question my life choices.

Dota 2 is an incredible game where teamwork, strategy and communication come together beautifully, usually for about 30 seconds before someone starts typing in all chat.

The toxicity is truly something special. You don't just play against the enemy team; you also fight your own teammates, your internet connection, your matchmaking luck, and occasionally your own sanity.

Still giving it a thumbs up because, despite the flaming, griefing, ping spam and the occasional teammate who appears to have been personally sent by Satan, there is nothing quite like a good Dota game.

My current strategy for staying sane is simple: mute everyone, trust nobody, and remember that it's only a game.

Then queue again 5 minutes later.

Dota 2: 10/10.
My mental health: pending.

testCases.rawText:
The current Dota 2 is clearly not the work of Ice Frog, but a typical valve style design

After version 7.0, the designer added new things that disrupted the high degree of freedom team design built by Ice Frog in its early days.

Striving to bind all players together and let one person who makes a mistake punish all those who don't, Valve calls it "teamwork", which is really humorous


This design is reflected in Blizzard's Storm Heroes, but it has already been featured in Valve's l4d1 or 2

However, this is a 'low degree of freedom team', and good design should provide players with multiple ways to give back to the team, rather than completing the designer's tasks. There should not be too many constraints between teammates, and tasks that can be completed by one person should not be forcibly assigned to two people. Let the strong lead the game to victory, rather than letting the weak drag one by four. Allowing the existence of 3v5 or even 2v5 like Dota1 is closer to a high degree of freedom team. And this is closer to the design concept of ice frogs.

testCases.rawText:
One of the greatest games ever created, played by some of the worst people ever created. 

While I love this game, I would never recommend it to somebody. 

In the open-beta days of DotA2 there was a different type of toxicity, the mindless vitriolic banter of MW2 or Halo 3 lobbies. Professional play did not exist in any meaningful capacity, stat tracking websites same, and MMR was hidden so any player in the game might be higher or lower ranked than yourself. In that era, the game felt truly magical. Once the numbers were added, people's attitudes shifted (indeed, even in unranked or turbo). The game became about increasing Epeen over defending the ancient. Playing off meta is met with immediate tantrums and feeding. Even with perfect behaviour and communication score. With the state of the game being what it is, I simply cannot recommend this game to others unless you yourself are a horrible person who would contribute to, and thrive in, the depraved temper tantrums that seem to have become the beating heart of DotA2. Luckily, the world is not short on pathetic emotional losers and thus DotA2 still lives. There is still a statistically relevant minority of the player base that actually enjoy dota and just mute the flamers and accept the coin flip of the tiny airlines being your mid vs the enemy's. 

This is the kind of game you just never walk away from, it is truly special. I got to attend The International in Shanghai this year and it was wonderful to see the DotA2 community alive and well and well into their 30s.
